stories.headline: Earthquake of Magnitude 7.0 Strikes Tibet; 16 Dead, 32 injured
stories.title: Earthquake of Magnitude 7.0 Strikes Tibet; 16 Dead, 32 injured
stories.summary: Tibet, October 23 : At least 16 people have died and 32 others have been injured after a magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck Tibet on Thursday, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported. According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the epicentre was located 183 km east-northeast of Nagqu city in Tibet. As per Xinhua, more than 300 houses have collapsed in the affected region, while the full extent of the damage is still being assessed. Rescue teams have been dispatched to the affected areas to carry out relief and rescue operations. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that railway authorities have suspended train services through the quake-hit areas following the earthquake. The National Centre for Seismology (NCS) on X stated, “The quake occurred at 20:03:43 IST at a depth of 173 km, with its epicentre at latitude 32.368 N and longitude 93.853 E, according to the NCS.” According to Xinhua's latest report published today, 11 of the 32 injured people were in serious condition, while 21 sustained minor injuries, as of 2:25 am (local time). More than 300 houses had collapsed in the affected region. The regional emergency command centre in Xizang has activated a Level-II emergency response to the earthquake to expedite rescue and relief operations in the affected areas. Further details are awaited.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

A magnitude-7.0 earthquake struck Tibet on Thursday, killing 16 people and injuring 32 others.
More than 300 houses collapsed, prompting rescue and relief operations.
Officials are assessing the damage as the region faces renewed concerns over disaster vulnerability.

Beijing, Oct 23: A magnitude 7 earthquake hit China's Tibet region on Thursday evening, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media said.
Search and rescue efforts continued following the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials.
More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts.
Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,000 tents and folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region.

The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 pm local time, with its epicentre 191 kilometres (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet.
The US agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10 kilometres (six miles), according to its website.
China's official news agency Xinhua said on Friday that communication in part of the region has been down.
Local railway authorities have taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region.

The earthquake also caused rockfalls that have forced local authorities to close a section of National Highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.
It was the biggest earthquake in the region in the last five years, China's national broadcaster CCTV said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work.

bullets.text: Intermittent snows are expected in the earthquake region over the next three days, Xinhua said.

stories.headline: UN climate fund provisionally earmarks $20 million for flood-hit Nepal
stories.title: UN climate fund provisionally earmarks $20 million for flood-hit Nepal
stories.summary: UN climate fund provisionally earmarks US$20 million for Nepal’s flood recovery
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) has provisionally set aside US$20 million for Nepal following devastating floods in August, offering limited financial support as the country faces a multibillion-dollar recovery bill.
The decision was taken at an extraordinary meeting of the fund’s board on Thursday.
Nepal will still have to submit a funding application, which the board is expected to consider at its next meeting in December.

Nepal’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment described the decision as approval of assistance worth approximately NPR 3 billion for relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction in affected communities.
The 26 August disaster struck the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli region, triggering floods and landslides that caused extensive destruction.
According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, more than 1,400 people were killed and over 5,000 remained unaccounted for.
Preliminary estimates indicated that around 60,000 people across 15,000 households were directly affected.
Assessments cited in the reports put economic losses and damage at between US$2.56 billion and US$2.69 billion, with recovery and reconstruction requirements estimated at US$4.71 billion.
The proposed funding would therefore meet less than 1 per cent of the estimated losses.
Agriculture, Forests and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary and Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle had jointly written to the fund on 31 August, requesting urgent assistance.
Several rounds of consultations involving representatives of developed and developing countries followed.

Raju Pandit Chhetri, lead climate finance negotiator for the least-developed countries at the UN climate negotiations, welcomed the decision as evidence that international cooperation could deliver a timely response to vulnerable countries.

stories.headline: Gutka Ban Bypassed as Twin Tobacco and Pan Masala Sachets Flood Assam Markets
stories.title: Gutka Ban Bypassed as Twin Tobacco and Pan Masala Sachets Flood Assam Markets
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Guwahati: The ban on sale, manufacture, storage, distribution, and transportation of gutka and pan masala containing tobacco or nicotine has apparently turned into a big joke in the country, including Assam.

For, the manufacturers and traders have found an ingenious way to bypass the prohibition - instead of selling as a single product, they have separated its ingredients and sell tobacco and pan masala in separate twin packs.
Consumers now mix them manually after purchase, thereby nullifying the very purpose of the ban.
Prior to the ban, tobacco, areca nut, nicotine and other ingredients were mixed with different flavours and sold as gutka.
Post the ban, companies have removed areca nut from the pack, selling it as a flavoured pan masala, while tobacco containing nicotine is sold in a separate sachet.
But when customers buy the two packets and mix them, the end product becomes a gutka, thus defeating the very essence of the ban.
The gravity of the fact can be gauged from the fact that the twin sachets of different brands are available in every nook and cranny of India, including Assam.
Though shopkeepers now don't display them openly, the twin sachet packets are nevertheless still sold in huge numbers.
Manufacturers too have found clever ways to sell their products.
For instance, some brands use surrogate marketing to trade their products - passing off pan masala as mouth fresheners to maintain market presence without explicitly promoting banned tobacco.
Meanwhile, the sale of gutka under a different avatar is taking a huge toll on public health in Assam.
Reports state that young people have been the worst affected, with 35% of the consumers being teenagers.

stories.headline: Cabinet Secretariat took no action on 2 Election Commissioners’ complaints against EC officer: RTI
stories.title: Cabinet Secretariat took no action on 2 Election Commissioners’ complaints against EC officer: RTI
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The complaints alleged that Maneesh Garg changed work allocations among senior poll officials without prior consultation or approval from the Election Commission.

New Delhi: The Cabinet Secretariat took no action on complaints sent by two Election Commissioners against the conduct of an officer in the Election Commission of India (ECI), stating that the communications were made in their “individual capacity” and that action without an official communication from the Commission as a whole could be inappropriate, documents released under the Right to Information (RTI) Act show.

Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had sent separate communications on July 29 to Cabinet Secretary T.V. Somanathan, raising concerns about the working of Senior Deputy Election Commissioner Maneesh Garg, an IAS officer posted to the Commission by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) on September 2, 2024.
The letters were provided in an RTI response to activist Commodore Lokesh K. Batra (retd).

The Indian Express had reported in September that Sandhu and Joshi wrote to the Cabinet Secretary after a work allocation order within the poll body raised concerns about the centralisation of powers to add or delete names and update records in electoral rolls, instead of allowing officials at the state level to handle these tasks.
In a statement on September 26, the Election Commission said the work redistribution orders issued by Garg had not been implemented following directions from the two Commissioners.
The poll panel also said the letters to the Cabinet Secretary concerned an officer on deputation, rather than policy or information technology division matters.
What did the Commissioners allege?

According to a Cabinet note included in the RTI response, both Commissioners alleged that Garg, after assuming charge as link officer of the Deputy Election Commissioner (Administration), issued an order changing work allocations among officers of equivalent or higher rank without consulting the Commission or the officers concerned.
They said the move came despite repeated oral and written instructions against making such changes without prior discussion or approval of the Commission.
The Commissioners alleged that Garg’s actions violated the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
Joshi also said that when he sought the relevant file from the Administration Division, it was not provided to him.

stories.headline: Cryosphere-related Hazards in the Himalaya
stories.title: Cryosphere-related Hazards in the Himalaya
stories.summary: The Himalaya is undergoing profound environmental transformation. Rising temperatures, retreating glaciers, degrading permafrost and changing precipitation patterns are reshaping mountain landscapes and increasing the potential for cascading hazards. Rock and ice avalanches, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), glacier detachments and extreme floods are no longer distant possibilities. They are immediate concerns for mountain communities, infrastructure planners and disaster management authorities. The catastrophic rock and ice avalanche at Chamoli, Uttarakhand, in February 2021 involved approximately 26 million m³ of material, comprising nearly 80% rock and 20% glacier ice, with the detached mass reaching a thickness of about 180 m. The collapse transformed into a destructive debris flow that swept through downstream valleys, destroying the Rishiganga hydropower project and severely damaging the Tapovan Vishnugad project, while claiming more than 200 lives or leaving people missing. A similar but much larger disaster struck the Rasuwa region of Nepal on 26 August 2026, when a rock and ice avalanche, preliminarily estimated at around 100 million m³, triggered a devastating flood that travelled more than 180 km downstream. The disaster affected 12 hydropower projects and resulted in at least 1,455 reported deaths, with hundreds more people missing in the aftermath. Originating near the Nepal-China border, the event also highlights the transboundary dimensions of mountain hazards, with consequences extending across interconnected river systems and infrastructure networks. Together, these disasters underscore the capacity of high mountain mass movements to trigger cascading impacts far downstream, often leaving communities and infrastructure with little time to respond. The October 2023 South Lhonak glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim exposed the cascading risks associated with rapidly changing cryospheric environments. The disaster involved a permafrost slope failure estimated at approximately 14 million m³, triggering a flood wave that displaced around 50 million m³ of water, while an estimated 270 million m³ of material was eroded along the channel. The resulting deluge devastated the Teesta River valley, destroyed the Teesta III hydropower project, and severely affected infrastructure and settlements along a 64 km stretch downstream, claiming more than 170 lives. Beyond its immediate impacts in India, the event underscored the transboundary implications of cryosphere-related hazards for downstream communities in Bangladesh. Such disasters demonstrate that hazards originating in remote glacial catchments can propagate across extensive river networks, threatening communities, infrastructure and livelihoods far beyond their source areas. In the Union Territory of Ladakh, the Gya GLOF of 2014 and other events highlight the vulnerability of mountain communities to sudden flood events. In this cold, arid region, streams are lifelines, sustaining villages, irrigation, and livelihoods. Their sudden transformation into destructive flood corridors can devastate agricultural land, damage infrastructure, and disrupt communities. Jammu and Kashmir faces its own set of cryosphere-related risks. Our recent study published in the Journal of Glaciology assessed 155 glacial lakes across the Kashmir Himalaya using satellite observations from 1992 to 2024. We documented a 26% increase in the area of ice contact proglacial lakes, while five lakes were classified as having very high GLOF susceptibility. The potential exposure includes thousands of buildings, 15 major bridges, roads, and a hydropower project. For Kashmir, these findings are a call for action. Potentially hazardous lakes and their downstream corridors must be identified, vulnerable settlements and infrastructure assessed, and early warning and evacuation systems strengthened. Scientific assessments must inform land use planning and infrastructure development before a disaster strikes, rather than being revisited only after lives and livelihoods have been lost. Hydropower development across the Himalaya, particularly along the Chenab River, warrants careful, science-based scrutiny. Small glacial lake outburst floods have also been documented in the Chenab basin, fortunately without reported impacts on hydropower infrastructure. However, the possibility of future events of substantially greater magnitude, potentially triggering cascading hazards, cannot be ruled out. Hydropower remains important for regional development and energy security, but powerhouses, access roads, tunnels and associated infrastructure must be planned with due consideration of upstream cryospheric hazards, unstable slopes, flood pathways and cascading impacts. Conventional engineering assessments alone may not adequately capture risks originating far upstream or evolving under a changing climate. Infrastructure resilience, therefore, requires integrated catchment-scale hazard assessments, scenario-based modelling and continuous monitoring for risk mitigation in increasingly dynamic mountain environments. The way forward requires a shift from reactive disaster management to anticipatory risk reduction. First, potentially hazardous glacial lakes, unstable slopes and vulnerable stream corridors must be systematically identified through satellite remote sensing, geophysical investigations and hydrodynamic modelling. Second, early warning systems must combine real-time lake and river monitoring, rainfall and seismic observations, reliable communication networks and community-based evacuation protocols. A warning system is effective only when the warning reaches people in time, and they know what to do. Third, development must respect the physical geography of mountain valleys. Based on recent experiences, a precautionary buffer of at least 300 meters along identified high-hazard stream corridors should be considered for restricting new infrastructure, subject to detailed geomorphological and flood modelling. This should not be interpreted as a universally safe or sufficient distance; actual exclusion zones must reflect the terrain and potential inundation extent. Ecozonation plans should guide settlements, roads, hydropower projects and tourism infrastructure away from high hazard areas. The use of geospatial artificial intelligence offers a powerful approach utilizing big data for detecting changes in glacial lakes, mapping unstable terrain, identifying exposed infrastructure and supporting scenario-based planning. However, these technologies must complement, not replace, field observations, engineering assessments and local knowledge. The message for this International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction is clear. These disasters are neither the first nor, certainly, the last. We cannot prevent every avalanche or outburst flood, but we can prevent avoidable exposure and reduce the loss of lives and livelihoods. The Himalaya needs development that respects its changing environment, informed by science, guided by precaution and centered on the safety of its people. Dr. Irfan Rashid is Associate Professor and Head, Department of Geoinformatics at the University of Kashmir. His research focuses on cryospheric processes, mountain hazards, and climate change in the Himalaya.

stories.headline: The Cage, the Keys, and the Command
stories.title: The Cage, the Keys, and the Command
stories.summary: Two years into Omar Abdullah’s government, its critics have chosen familiar trenches. One side lists broken promises, the other revisits the National Conference’s old sins. Both are partisan. Neither is a ledger. A fair ledger asks three questions of every promise. Was it within his authority? If not, what did he do about it? If it was, why is there a gap? A commander answers for what lies within his command, and for what he does about the rest. Applied honestly, the test clears Omar Abdullah of some charges and convicts him of others. The government has been honest about the cage, but not yet about the unlocked doors. Statehood, Article 370, the Public Safety Act, police and public order are not in the Chief Minister’s gift. Grading him on them grades the wrong man. A July 2024 amendment strengthened the Lieutenant Governor’s hold over police, public order, All India Services officers and prosecution sanctions. The cabinet’s business rules, approved in March 2025, remain unsettled after the LG returned them with queries. In April 2025, the LG transferred 48 JKAS officers while those rules were pending. Omar has said that SKIMS, the universities and the Power Development Corporation now sit with the unelected side. The purse is no freer. Of the ₹1.27 lakh crore budget for 2026–27, only about ₹31,800 crore is expected from the government’s own resources. Of ₹90,018 crore in projected revenue receipts, ₹58,218 crore, about 65 per cent, is expected as central grants. On statehood, the Centre has offered no timeframe. Omar has met Amit Shah five times and been told, in effect, “at an appropriate time.” He has said the PSA will go by ordinance the day full powers return. A Union Territory assembly cannot legislate on police or public order at all. A BJP spokesman has demanded a two-year report card. The largest unmet promise on that card is one only the BJP’s government can keep. Yet where authority lies with the elected government, the record is more mixed. Power, recruitment, daily-wage regularisation and targeted welfare show delay, dilution or incomplete delivery. Omar holds the Power and Finance portfolios himself. From 1 September 2026, electricity tariffs rose by an average of 6.83 per cent, even as Kashmir faces a winter shortfall of roughly 800 MW. The promised 200 free units were narrowed to Antyodaya households, about 2.23 lakh families. The Centre cleared the scheme in February 2026; by September, vendors were still being evaluated. On jobs, the manifesto promised vacancies filled within 180 days. JKPSC advertised 357 posts in 2025–26 against 2,586 in 2023–24; JKSSB advertised 1,731 against 5,044 in 2024–25. Advertised posts are not appointments, and the earlier figures largely belong to the LG’s administration. Even so, the direction is wrong, and the 180-day promise remains distant. Daily wagers are the starkest case. A committee under the Chief Secretary was formed in March 2025 with six months to report. Its report has not been tabled, and estimates of the workforce range from over 50,000 to over a lakh. Whatever needs the LG’s signature, this file has not yet reached his desk. LPG relief has shrunk from twelve free cylinders to six, for Antyodaya households only, and there is no sign of the promised ₹5,000 a month for women who head poor households. The ledger, however, is not blank. His March 2025 budget was the first presented by an elected government in seven years, and the 2026–27 budget followed on schedule. Free bus travel for women began within months of the promise. Marriage assistance for girls from Antyodaya households rose from ₹50,000 to ₹75,000. The Darbar Move was restored. Mission YUVA shows activity. By 31 August 2026, it had received 1,00,407 applications and disbursed 32,156 loans. Those are loans, not jobs. The scheme is a real administrative achievement, but not yet an employment outcome. Its success must be judged by enterprise survival and hiring, not disbursement alone. The railway link to Kashmir was begun decades before this government took office. Its completion falls in this tenure, but the credit does not. Zuhaib Yusuf Mir’s charge of “surrender” is rhetoric. The government passed two Assembly resolutions and, in July, took its demand to Delhi, where police stopped the Chief Minister short of the protest venue. But his question about sequencing deserves an answer. Omar gave the Centre nearly two years of quiet talks before announcing the “Delhi Chalo” campaign. The September 2026 resolution sought full statehood alone, and he urged his members not to press amendments on special status. That was tactically defensible, since it denied the BJP an easy pretext. But it also confirmed a strategic retreat, from restoration of special status and autonomy to the narrower demand for statehood. The electorate has noticed. The National Conference lost Budgam, its first defeat there since 1977, while its own MP, Aga Ruhullah Mehdi, stayed out of the campaign. Patience with New Delhi has bought no timeline, and dissent at home is growing. The ledger must also be regional. A government elected across Jammu and Kashmir cannot measure itself only by Srinagar’s political anxieties or the Valley’s grievances. Jammu’s voters will ask whether power supply, recruitment, daily-wage regularisation and development funds have reached their districts with the same urgency. The Darbar Move may have been restored, but restoration of a ritual is not restoration of regional confidence. If Delhi has clipped the government’s wings, it must still explain why the powers it possesses have not been used with equal energy in Jammu, Chenab Valley, Pir Panjal and the Kashmir Valley alike. Sunil Sethi’s history of the National Conference and the Congress is a debate for another day. It does not tell a daily wager, twenty years in service, whether his file is moving. Nor does it excuse a Centre that holds the key to statehood. The government has three years left. It should publish a public scorecard: every manifesto promise, the department responsible, the order or budget line behind it, the number of beneficiaries and the date. Where the LG or Centre holds the key, the scorecard should say so. Where Omar holds it, it should say that too. This would answer critics better than another resolution and oblige adversaries to argue facts. Delhi holds the key to statehood. Omar holds the keys to recruitment, power, welfare and the daily wager’s file. He may blame the cage. He cannot blame every unlocked door. Responsibility without authority is an injustice; authority without accountability is negligence. This government may protest the first, but it must answer for the second. opening: Two years into Omar Abdullah’s government, its critics have chosen familiar trenches.
One side lists broken promises, the other revisits the National Conference’s old sins.
body: Both are partisan.
Neither is a ledger.
A fair ledger asks three questions of every promise.
Was it within his authority?
If not, what did he do about it?
If it was, why is there a gap?
A commander answers for what lies within his command, and for what he does about the rest.
Applied honestly, the test clears Omar Abdullah of some charges and convicts him of others.
The government has been honest about the cage, but not yet about the unlocked doors.
Statehood, Article 370, the Public Safety Act, police and public order are not in the Chief Minister’s gift.
Grading him on them grades the wrong man.
A July 2024 amendment strengthened the Lieutenant Governor’s hold over police, public order, All India Services officers and prosecution sanctions.
The cabinet’s business rules, approved in March 2025, remain unsettled after the LG returned them with queries.
In April 2025, the LG transferred 48 JKAS officers while those rules were pending.
Omar has said that SKIMS, the universities and the Power Development Corporation now sit with the unelected side.
The purse is no freer.
Of ₹90,018 crore in projected revenue receipts, ₹58,218 crore, about 65 per cent, is expected as central grants.
On statehood, the Centre has offered no timeframe.
Omar has met Amit Shah five times and been told, in effect, “at an appropriate time.” He has said the PSA will go by ordinance the day full powers return.
A Union Territory assembly cannot legislate on police or public order at all.
A BJP spokesman has demanded a two-year report card.
The largest unmet promise on that card is one only the BJP’s government can keep.
Yet where authority lies with the elected government, the record is more mixed.
Power, recruitment, daily-wage regularisation and targeted welfare show delay, dilution or incomplete delivery.
Omar holds the Power and Finance portfolios himself.
From 1 September 2026, electricity tariffs rose by an average of 6.83 per cent, even as Kashmir faces a winter shortfall of roughly 800 MW.
The promised 200 free units were narrowed to Antyodaya households, about 2.23 lakh families.
The Centre cleared the scheme in February 2026; by September, vendors were still being evaluated.
On jobs, the manifesto promised vacancies filled within 180 days.
JKPSC advertised 357 posts in 2025–26 against 2,586 in 2023–24; JKSSB advertised 1,731 against 5,044 in 2024–25.
Advertised posts are not appointments, and the earlier figures largely belong to the LG’s administration.
Even so, the direction is wrong, and the 180-day promise remains distant.
Daily wagers are the starkest case.
A committee under the Chief Secretary was formed in March 2025 with six months to report.
Its report has not been tabled, and estimates of the workforce range from over 50,000 to over a lakh.
Whatever needs the LG’s signature, this file has not yet reached his desk.
LPG relief has shrunk from twelve free cylinders to six, for Antyodaya households only, and there is no sign of the promised ₹5,000 a month for women who head poor households.
The ledger, however, is not blank.
His March 2025 budget was the first presented by an elected government in seven years, and the 2026–27 budget followed on schedule.
Free bus travel for women began within months of the promise.
Marriage assistance for girls from Antyodaya households rose from ₹50,000 to ₹75,000.
The Darbar Move was restored.
Mission YUVA shows activity.
By 31 August 2026, it had received 1,00,407 applications and disbursed 32,156 loans.
Those are loans, not jobs.
The scheme is a real administrative achievement, but not yet an employment outcome.
Its success must be judged by enterprise survival and hiring, not disbursement alone.
The railway link to Kashmir was begun decades before this government took office.
Its completion falls in this tenure, but the credit does not.
Zuhaib Yusuf Mir’s charge of “surrender” is rhetoric.
The government passed two Assembly resolutions and, in July, took its demand to Delhi, where police stopped the Chief Minister short of the protest venue.
But his question about sequencing deserves an answer.
Omar gave the Centre nearly two years of quiet talks before announcing the “Delhi Chalo” campaign.
The September 2026 resolution sought full statehood alone, and he urged his members not to press amendments on special status.
That was tactically defensible, since it denied the BJP an easy pretext.
But it also confirmed a strategic retreat, from restoration of special status and autonomy to the narrower demand for statehood.
The electorate has noticed.
The National Conference lost Budgam, its first defeat there since 1977, while its own MP, Aga Ruhullah Mehdi, stayed out of the campaign.
Patience with New Delhi has bought no timeline, and dissent at home is growing.
The ledger must also be regional.
A government elected across Jammu and Kashmir cannot measure itself only by Srinagar’s political anxieties or the Valley’s grievances.
Jammu’s voters will ask whether power supply, recruitment, daily-wage regularisation and development funds have reached their districts with the same urgency.
The Darbar Move may have been restored, but restoration of a ritual is not restoration of regional confidence.
If Delhi has clipped the government’s wings, it must still explain why the powers it possesses have not been used with equal energy in Jammu, Chenab Valley, Pir Panjal and the Kashmir Valley alike.
Sunil Sethi’s history of the National Conference and the Congress is a debate for another day.
It does not tell a daily wager, twenty years in service, whether his file is moving.
Nor does it excuse a Centre that holds the key to statehood.
The government has three years left.
It should publish a public scorecard: every manifesto promise, the department responsible, the order or budget line behind it, the number of beneficiaries and the date.
Where the LG or Centre holds the key, the scorecard should say so.
Where Omar holds it, it should say that too.
This would answer critics better than another resolution and oblige adversaries to argue facts.
